title: Choose rounding mode when casting to dtype
github_labels: module: cuda|triaged|module: type promotion|function request|oncall: pt2|module: inductor|module: floatx (formerly float8)|bot-triaged
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch `tensor.to(dtype)` performs a round-nearest conversion. This makes sense in most cases, but there are situations where other rounding modes are useful. For example in MXFP8 (microscaled float8) on Blackwell GPUs, we need to convert the scales to their next power of 2 and convert them to a float8_e8m0fnu (i.e., a biased uint8). This could be done in one shot via `scales.to(torch.float8_e8m0fnu, round="up")`. Which then would allow PyTorch to match this exactly to the optimized PTX instruction `cvt.rp.satfinite.ue8m0x2.f32` (`.rp` means round-positive). ### Alternatives Several less-readable alternatives, which will also make it harder for PyTorch and Inductor to understand the intent and thus optimize the code. For example one could go through torch.log and torch.ceil, or through torch.frexp, or do the cast with round-nearest and the conditionally adjust the result. ### Additional context _No response_ cc @ptrblck @msaroufim @eqy @jerryzh168 @tinglvv @nWEIdia @nairbv @mruberry @voznesenskym @penguinwu @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @ipiszy @kadeng @muchulee8 @amjames @chauhang @aak...

title: Stream-k matmul implementation very slow mostly because of if/else inside for loop
body_excerpt: These last days I tried to implement the paper [Stream-K: Work-centric Parallel Decomposition for Dense Matrix-Matrix Multiplication on the GPU](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.03598.pdf) in Triton. The main idea is to avoid wave quantization by evenly distributing work across SM using a lower granularity than a full tile. I suppose you have seen/read it, if not I can share my notes about it to help understand what I hope to achieve. It has been implemented in cutlass where it shows strong performances. The implementation below in Triton works, aka it generates the right output (minus rounding issues when K is big because of half precision, nothing unexpected). It corresponds to the `two-tile Stream-K + data-parallel` hybrid schedule from the paper: - during the first stage, each SM gets the equivalent work of more 1 full tile plus the work which would have led to quantization wave (the last wave in tiled base matmul), such that every SM does almost the same quantity of work. title: truncated_normal can't handle extreme bounds
body_excerpt: `jax.random.truncated_normal` produces deeply wrong results when you set the lower bound too high or the upper bound too low. For example, ```python jax.random.truncated_normal( jax.random.PRNGKey(1), jnp.array([5., 5.25, 5.5]), 1e6, (3,)) ``` results in ``` DeviceArray([5.1665773e+00, 9.9999994e+05, 9.9999994e+05], dtype=float32) ``` The transition is suspiciously close to the point at which `erf` runs out of precision: ```python lax.erf(jnp.array([5., 5.25, 5.5]) / np.sqrt(2)) ``` gives ``` DeviceArray([0.9999994, 1. , 1. ], dtype=float32) ``` So this may be a fundamental limitation of the sampling-by-inversion scheme used in `truncated_normal`.

title: Inconsistent Reduction precision in backwards computation
body_excerpt: ### Description JAX implicitly upcasts BF16 inputs to `jnp.sum` to FP32 (see [here](https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/955f96a453184441d6db11261eab40f24131b1ef/jax/_src/numpy/reductions.py#L231)). title: Ctx or at least Thread level switch for fp32 IEEE precision tolerance
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Right now fp precision switching is only possible at the `process` level via the following api: ```python torch.backends.fp32_precision = mode torch.backends.cuda.matmul.fp32_precision = mode torch.backends.cudnn.fp32_precision = mode torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision = mode torch.backends.cudnn.rnn.fp32_precision = mode ``` With Python 3.13/3.14 and `GIL=0` threads, it is now possile to do everything `torch.distributed` can do but using threads instead of processes. Without a `ctx` or `thread` level toggle for `fp` precision, it not possible to have different threads doing different tasks. For example, an `inference` thread does not need high precision whereas a `quantization` thread which often need fp32 or higher accumulation will need full `ieee` precision. They cannot co-exist currently in torch due to this limitation. ### Alternatives Use `processes`. However, this is not a true alternative since with Python 3.14, we have stable `nogil` threads that can do concurrent work as efficiently if not more so than `processes`. cc @svekars @sekyondaMeta @AlannaBurke @ptrblck @msaroufim @eqy @jerryzh168 @albanD @pragupta

body_excerpt: I'd like to be able to use cuML to calculate the precision score of an estimator in Python. title: Disentangle "jax_enable_x64" and default dtype
body_excerpt: ### Description Providing a way to enable `float64` without changing the default dtype/precision. Or even better, adding the option to choose the default dtype. For example, ```python jax.config.update('jax_enable_x64', True) jax.config.update('jax_default_dtype', jnp.float32) ``` ### Motivation Some algorithms, such as fast Fourier transforms and conjugate gradient methods, are unstable at 32-bit precision. It is therefore recommended to apply them at 64-bit precision. If such algorithms are part of some bigger procedure, the entire procedure must run at 64-bit precision. This is very wasteful, especially if the procedure involves neural networks. The current solution is to rewrite the procedure while explicitly requesting the `float32` dtype at **every** array creation. For large code bases, this is very tedious and it prevents the use of most libraries. ### Alternatives An even better solution would be to be able to set the dtype locally (e.g. with contexts), but I suspect that this would not play well with tracers.

title: jax.lax.linalg.lu returns LU factorisation for singular matrix, jax.scipy.linalg.lu_solve silently returns spurious result in 32bit
body_excerpt: ### Description Singular matrix with linearly dependent columns have infinitely many LU factorisations. title: DeepSeek: mixed precision optimizers (BF16AdamW)
body_excerpt: DeepSeek mentions that they keep optimizer states in bf16, this is something that afaik our optimizers don't support. Similarly, one could imagine computing/accumulating gradients in less than fp32 accuracy and adding them to fp32 params, something that's also not supported today, when `param` and `param.grad` are mandated to have the same dtype, and by default optimizers operate on `param` and `param.grad`. title: [MPS] For accumulating ops allow the correctness tolerance to scale within the envelope of the reference implementations drift
body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug ### Context Related to the discussion at issue #182817 this is an orthogonal issue with the current testing approach and a suggestion on how we could address it: When testing op correctness for fp16/bf16 implementations in MPS backend we compare against the CPU computations done with the same precision. For ops that aggregate multiple computations to produce the elements of the final result like convolutions or reduction ops the ordering how the computation happens will cause a drift in the final product. One can estimate the worst case per-element error with `err = sqrt(K) * eps * |x|` where `K` is the reduction depth, `eps` the machine epsilon for the dtype and `|x|` the partial product magnitude. title: Raise exception when torch.clamp min value underflows the input tensor's dtype
body_excerpt: Consider the following code: ```python x = torch.relu(torch.randn(10)) x = torch.clamp(x, min=1e-8) y = 100 / x ``` The code above runs just fine when `x.dtype == torch.float` but fails when `x.dtype == torch.half`. The error is that 1e-8 can't be represented in fp16 and silently underflows to 0. title: thrust sort/argsort silently produces wrong results when workspace allocation fails
body_excerpt: ## Summary `cupy.sort()` and `cupy.argsort()` can silently return incorrect results when GPU memory is under pressure and thrust workspace allocation fails. The root cause is that `cupy/cuda/thrust.pyx` declares `cupy_malloc()` as `noexcept with gil`. When `memory.alloc()` raises `OutOfMemoryError`, Cython swallows the exception, prints a warning to stderr, and returns NULL. The C++ allocator does not validate this NULL pointer, so thrust receives a garbage workspace buffer, silently corrupts the sort output, and returns normally without raising an exception. ## Expected Behavior `cupy.sort()` and `cupy.argsort()` should raise `OutOfMemoryError` when thrust workspace allocation fails, preventing silent data corruption. ## Actual Behavior When VRAM utilization crosses a threshold (varies by GPU architecture): - A message is printed to stderr: `Exception ignored in: 'cupy.cuda.thrust.cupy_malloc'` followed by the full `OutOfMemoryError` traceback - The `sort()` / `argsort()` call returns **without raising an exception** - The returned array contains **incorrect values** - Downstream computation silently uses corrupted results ## Environment | Property | Value | |----------|-------...

title: pjit uses too much memory
body_excerpt: ### Description Suppose I have a large state stored on CPU, and a tree of shardings matching the state structure. Let's assume the partition is fairly uniform, so that about the same amount of memory should supposedly be allocated per device after sharding. title: [TASK] Increase parallelism or sparse normalization prims
body_excerpt: Cuml has CSR-based primitives that contain kernels, both in Python and in C, which currently map each row of the CSR to a single thread and loop over the columns serially to perform L1/l2/l_inf normalization. The performance and the parallelism, including the sums, could be made much more parallel if we map the individual rows to warps with a block size set to something like the average degree. The current method might be the best option when the average degree is extremely small but as the average degree grows larger, the parallelism can be increased significantly, while also enabling coalesced reads (and potentially even writes in the case of normalization where all the values need to be modified).

title: jaxlib: malformed pickled PyTreeDef can crash flatten_up_to
body_excerpt: `PyTreeDef` pickle state includes cached per-node bookkeeping fields: ```text (kind, arity, node_data, custom_type, num_leaves, num_nodes) ``` `PyTreeDef.__setstate__` / `FromPickle` currently restores those cached `num_leaves` and `num_nodes` values directly. title: ROCM build fails when the ROCM_PATH is a symlinked location
body_excerpt: ### Description The jaxlib build with ROCm will fail if the ROCM_PATH is directed to a symlinked location. This issue is particularly critical for NixOS, as the ROCM_PATH is invariably a symlinked location joining each individual library together, thereby making ROCM build on NixOS unfeasible. While this may be less significant for other distributions, it is still a common issue, given that /opt/rocm is likely to be a symlink. title: feat(examples): implement vllm in triton
body_excerpt: Vllm uses paged memory and has kernels that perform the generation part of the causal inference. The computation pattern of generation part - single Q for entire seq len of KV - is very different from computing the context part (which benefits from seq length parallelism over Q and hence flash attention). In this case, the bottleneck should be memory, as the KV values cannot be reused over the Q seq len, so it is an interesting question to ask how to tradeoff latency and parallelism with compute efficiency. In this case, batching similar seq length inference is very important. I also wonder if distributed shared memory and TMA optimizations would be beneficial here since it is so memory-bottlenecked. It would be interesting to implement this in triton and see whether triton can match or exceed the performance. Reference VLLM implementation here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/d2b2eed67c49cdda3c1d6fa09ee2ec128b318138/csrc/attention/attention_kernels.cu#L32

title: [Bug] Padded, quantized convolution operators give incorrect results on edges
body_excerpt: When the microTVM team was working on our submission for MLPerf Tiny, we noticed the `kws` model had slightly worse accuracy than expected (we classified `897/1000` samples correctly, while folks are expected to classify [at least `900/1000` correctly](https://github.com/mlcommons/tiny/tree/master/benchmark)). The bug has been remarkably hard to track down. We have a bunch of [end-to-end operator](https://github.com/apache/tvm/tree/main/tests/python/relay/strategy/arm_cpu/) tests, and our results match exactly with those in other parts of TVM. I originally thought this was a padding issue, but that didn't pan out. It turns out the issue is caused by a bugged optimization for re-quantization. This issue only occurs in quantization (which is why our tests didn't catch it - those don't include quantization steps), and only on the edges of padded tensors (which explains why it hurt accuracy slightly, but not a ton). I've written up an explanation of the issue below. cc @alanmacd @areusch @gromero @mehrdadh @mkatanbaf

title: Result caching in Numba
body_excerpt: This issue serves as a backup of some ideas discussed in the Gitter room. # Result caching in combination with Numba ## Premise One clear application of numba is the speedup of costly computations. Besides acceleration of such computations, it could be useful to cache results of such functions, if they are pure functions and expected to be called with the same parameters frequently. The Python standard library offers e.g. the [lru_cache in the functools module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.lru_cache), which memoises the most recent calls of the functions it is wrapping. ## Challenge At the current time, no best practice or recipe exists for how to efficiently combine numba's jit capabilities and a caching approach. title: [Tracking Issue][TFLite] Support quantized operator import in Relax frontend
body_excerpt: ## Problem The Relax TFLite frontend currently has two related blockers for quantized TFLite import. First, quantized tensors are blocked early in `get_tensors()` by the tensor quantization metadata guard. After preserving tensor-level quantization metadata (`scale`, `zero_point`, and `axis`) and allowing the frontend to proceed further, the next blocker appears at the operator conversion stage: ```text NameError: name '_qnn' is not defined ``` This happens because the frontend contains quantized operator conversion paths that reference non-existent `_qnn.op.*` APIs. At the same time, Relax already provides `quantize` / `dequantize` operators with C++ registration, Python APIs, legalization to TE, and tests. This suggests that quantized TFLite operators may initially be imported using QDQ decomposition around existing Relax ops, rather than requiring a new set of fused QNN operators as the first step. This issue tracks the work needed to support quantized TFLite operator import in the Relax frontend. ## Affected `_qnn.op.*` calls The TFLite frontend (`python/tvm/relax/frontend/tflite/tflite_frontend.py`) references 7 non-existent QNN ops across 18 call sites: | Op | Call sites |...

title: [AMD] Enable BufferOps Support with tl.make_block_ptr

Normally this seems to be the purpose of `CanonicalizePointers`, but this approach doesn't work because the specified vector section of the offsets are already in int64 due to the implicit casting from the API. title: Wrongly returns nan for vectorized complex numbers division on PPC/ZArch
body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug Copied from #92043 which still applies for vectorized PPC and likely to ZArch while it was fixed for x86 by #93277 Pytorch wrongly returns nan for complex numbers division where the results are still within the range of the datatype. title: Support alpha=inf consistently for torch.celu
body_excerpt: The celu activation function introduced in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1704.07483 is described as being C1 differentiable across values of alpha. - for alpha -> inf it converges to the identity op (f(x) = x) - for alpha -> 0+ it converges to relu(x) = max(0, x) The Pytorch [celu](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/aten/src/ATen/native/Activation.cpp#L538-L549) (and related [quantized_celu](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/aten/src/ATen/native/quantized/cpu/qelu.cpp#L24)) ) implementation(s) appears to call a parameterized elu, following the celu definition, so it looks like it will have these properties within bounds of overflow. On the other hand I am not sure what the Pytorch behavior is intended to be in the implementation for alpha=0 and alpha=inf, but I think it would be nice to have it consistent. At alpha=0 it raises RuntimeError ZeroDivisionError, which is fine, though it seems could instead for alpha=0 just short-circuit to return relu(x). On the other hand, at alpha=torch.inf, positive values of x appear to return x, while non-positive values of x return `torch.nan`: ``` x = torch.tensor(2.) torch.celu(x, torch.inf) # tensor(2.) torch.celu(-x, torch.inf...

title: [MPS] Complex `abs` overflows/underflows with large/small inputs
github_labels: module: numerical-stability|triaged|module: complex|module: edge cases|module: mps|bot-triaged
body_excerpt: For sufficiently large or small complex inputs, the output of `torch.abs` for MPS overflows to inf or underflows to 0, whereas the CPU op does not. This is due to the fact that the formula that the MPS op uses is $\sqrt{\text{real}^2 + \text{imag}^2}$, so the square can overflow. Reproducer: ```python import torch a_cpu = torch.tensor( [ 1e-30 + 1e-30j, 1e32 + 1e32j, ], device='cpu', dtype=torch.cfloat, ) a_mps = a_cpu.to('mps') a_cpu_abs = a_cpu.abs() a_mps_abs = a_mps.abs() print(f'{a_cpu=}') print(f'{a_mps=}') print(f'{a_cpu_abs=}') print(f'{a_mps_abs=}') ``` Running the above gives: ``` a_cpu=tensor([1.0000e-30+1.0000e-30j, 1.0000e+32+1.0000e+32j]) a_mps=tensor([1.0000e-30+1.0000e-30j, 1.0000e+32+1.0000e+32j], device='mps:0') a_cpu_abs=tensor([1.4142e-30, 1.4142e+32]) a_mps_abs=tensor([0., inf], device='mps:0') ``` cc @ezyang @anjali411 @dylanbespalko @mruberry @nikitaved @amjames @kulinseth @malfet @DenisVieriu97 @jhavukainen @aditvenk

title: Ban GradScaler scale from being less than 1
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch We should standardize on a way to tell users when a reasonable/good scale for the AMP GradScaler cannot be found. Context: The grad scaler is awesome in that it "automatically" finetunes itself to settle on an ideal scale. However! There are instances where there is just no ideal scale for certain parameters, for example the one mentioned in issue #96755, where the scale becomes so so tiny that it causes infs and, consequently, nans. In this issue, we were nestled in the unlikely (but clearly not impossible) world where for a certain scale S, the scaled gradients were valid, but the unscaled (g/S) were invalid, leading to weird inconsistent behavior. Generally, we want to be add invariants/guarantees to prevent weird inconsistent behavior and give users faster and clearer signal. Since the purpose of the scale is to scale UP the loss so that the grads do not underflow in fp16, we should set a hard boundary of scale must be greater than or equal to 1. title: jnp.log/log2/log10 return -inf for subnormal float32 inputs (XLA DAZ flush)
body_excerpt: ### Description `jnp.log`, `jnp.log2`, and `jnp.log10` return `-inf` for subnormal `float32` inputs on the CPU backend, while NumPy returns the correct finite negative values. title: `softmax` to handle dimensions comprised of `-inf`
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Currently `softmax` handles `-inf` in most of the cases, for example: ```python >>> x = torch.tensor([-float('inf'), 1]) >>> x.softmax(-1) tensor([0., 1.]) >>> x.cuda().softmax(-1) tensor([0., 1.], device='cuda:0') ``` However, once the normalized dimension is comprised of solely `-inf`, there is an issue: ```python >>> x = torch.tensor([-float('inf')] * 2) >>> x.softmax(-1) tensor([nan, nan]) >>> x.cuda().softmax(-1) tensor([nan, nan], device='cuda:0') ``` I understand we get it because `inf - inf = nan`, but why not assume that `softmax` is computed in the limit? In such a case `softmax` should return a uniform distribution. This case is quite easy to detect since `max == -inf` will imply a uniform distribution. Issues for more context: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/25110 https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/103749 https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/103963 cc @albanD @mruberry @jbschlosser @walterddr @mikaylagawarecki

title: Should gradients of logsumexp([-inf, -inf]) be 0s instead NaNs?

title: Implicit dtype promotion for float8 and int4
body_excerpt: We've had several requests to add implicit promotion semantics for float8, int4, and friends. What do i mean by this? Currently, if you try to combine `float8` with other float dtypes in binary operations, you get an error: ```python >>> jnp.float8_e3m4(1) + jnp.bfloat16(1) TypePromotionError: Input dtypes ('bfloat16', 'float8_e3m4') have no available implicit dtype promotion path. To avoid unintended promotion, 8-bit floats do not support implicit promotion. If you'd like your inputs to be promoted to another type, you can do so explicitly using e.g. x.astype('float32') ``` This was a deliberate design choice: when we first added narrow-width floats and ints, our assumption was that they would mostly be used in very particular settings, e.g. as inputs to device-specific matmul kernels, and users would benefit from having guard-rails against inadvertent type promotion. title: Request to support fp8 x4 packed dtypes in PT
body_excerpt: Trainium3 hardware natively operates on packed FP8 dtypes: float8_e4m3fn_x4 and float8_e5m2_x4, which bundle 4 FP8 elements into 1 logical element along the free dimension. Example: a float8_e4m3fn tensor of shape [64, 128] becomes a float8_e4m3fn_x4 tensor of shape [64, 32] given -1 is the free dim. Currently, we handle this packing/unpacking internally in our kernels, but we'd like to propose adding these two x4 dtypes to PT Core. cc @jerryzh168 @jianyuh @raghuramank100 @jamesr66a @vkuzo @jgong5 @Xia-Weiwen @leslie-fang-intel

title: [CUDA][CUDACachingAllocator] size overflow in caching_allocator_alloc raises SystemError for size >= 2**63

body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug ### Describe the bug `torch.cuda.memory.caching_allocator_alloc()` raises a `SystemError` when the requested allocation size is `2**63`. For `2**63`, it raises: ```text SystemError: _cuda_cudaCachingAllocator_raw_alloc returned a result with an exception set ``` I think this is not expected behavior. title: Inaccurate complex tanh implementation
body_excerpt: Numba complex tanh implementation returns nans for large real values, probably due to some intermediate under/overflow. The following code fails: ``` import numpy as np import numba @numba.jit def numba_tanh(x): return np.tanh(x) points = [-700+1j, 700+1j] for x in points: expected = np.tanh(x) got = numba_tanh(x) np.testing.assert_allclose(got, expected) ``` (tested on Numba 0.37.0, didn't test on 0.38.0 since llvmlite 0.23 failed to work out of the box on fedora 28) Replacing `np.tanh` with `cmath.tanh` in `numba_tanh` does work however.

title: Semi-surprising type promotion of float literals vs scalars
body_excerpt: I hit a surprising behavior in type promotion, and I wanted to get some feedback on whether it's intentional. title: [FEA] Changing `COO` `Index_Type` in UMAP to prevent overflow when running with large datasets
body_excerpt: ### Description UMAP cannot run large datasets right now because of an overflow issue. `raft::sparse::COO` defaults to using `int` for its `Index_Type` and this becomes a problem. When [this issue](https://github.com/rapidsai/raft/issues/2405) is solved, we need to update `UMAPAlgo::FuzzySimplSet::ML::run()` to take `COO` with an `Index_Type` other than `int`. ### Details Specifically, `coo_symmetrize` (raft function called from `UMAPAlgo::FuzzySimplSet::ML::run()`) allocates `nnz * 2` space on device. For a large dataset (e.g. 88M samples with knn graph degree 16) this value is larger than max int (88M * 16 * 2 > INT_MAX).

title: dict_tag optimization leads to wrong results with relational guards
body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug `dict_tag` optimization checks if a dictionary that we guard on has changed or not and if all the values in it are immutable, no further processing is done on the dictionary if the tag is the same. This avoids running a lot of guards on the dictionary and its values and makes the C++ guards faster. However this assumes that running a guard has no side-effects. This is true for almost all cases except for RelationalGuards which do keep a state. In RelationalGuards, we need 2 values for the guards and the way it works is that the guard returns True for the first run, stores the first value in the guard and only returns True or False in the last run. When a guard is not run because of dict_tag optimization, this leads to false positives. Eg: ```python import torch a = torch.randn(5).cuda() d = {"a": a} def fn(a, d): return a is d["a"], torch.sum(a) cfn = torch.compile(fn) print(cfn(a, d)[0]) print(cfn(a.clone(), d)[0]) ``` Above prints `True` in both cases because of the dict_tag optimization. title: Missing bounds check in round_size() causes zero-size block and double allocation

body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug  # Missing bounds check in `round_size()` causes zero-size block and double allocation  ## 🐛 Describe the bug  `round_size()` in `c10/cuda/CUDACachingAllocator.cpp` (line 2888) does an unchecked `size_t` addition:  ```cpp return kMinBlockSize * ((size + kMinBlockSize - 1) / kMinBlockSize); ```  For `size` values in the range `[SIZE_MAX - 510, SIZE_MAX]`, `size + 511` wraps to zero in C++ unsigned arithmetic, so `round_size()` returns `0`. Currently our mnmg kmeans implementation performs a copy of the input partitions in order to concatenate the partitions on each workers into a single partition. title: Numerical Discrepancies between Pallas Kernel and Standard JAX with bfloat16
body_excerpt: ### Description We are observing small numerical differences between a JAX function compiled with @jax.jit and an equivalent operation implemented as a Pallas kernel when using jnp.bfloat16 data types. The operations involve taking the mean of the squares of a tiled 2D array row-wise, followed by a reciprocal square root. While all intermediate computations within both versions are explicitly cast to jnp.float32, the final results, when cast back to jnp.bfloat16, show differences in a small number of elements. The standard JAX version and the Pallas kernel version produce bit-identical results when the input and output types are jnp.float32. The discrepancies only appear when downcasting the float32 results to jnp.bfloat16.
